phrases.explanation: Muslims begin Qur’an recitation with this phrase, placing the words that follow under Allah’s name and seeking His blessing and help. It shifts attention from the speaker’s own ability to the One being addressed. The same opening is used before many ordinary actions, linking daily life with remembrance of Allah.

The Arabic name al-Raḥmān conveys vast mercy that reaches creation. It appears throughout the Qur’an, including the opening of many surahs. Here it describes the One whose name the worshipper has just invoked. The prayer begins not with bargaining but with recognition of Allah’s mercy.

Together with the previous name, al-Raḥīm reinforces that Allah’s mercy is not a passing kindness but a quality by which He is known. The two names are often paired in Qur’anic openings, surrounding recitation with hope before any request is made. Later the Qur’an tells those who have wronged themselves, “Do not despair of Allah’s mercy” (39:53), echoing that hope.

Praise here includes more than saying thank you: it recognizes what is excellent and gives its deepest credit to Allah. A hadith qudsi in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim describes al-Fātiḥah as an exchange between Allah and His servant. When the servant praises the Lord of all worlds, Allah answers that the servant has praised Him.

This wording directs praise to Allah as its ultimate source, since life, ability, and provision depend on Him. It does not cancel gratitude to people. The Prophet Muhammad taught that whoever is not grateful to people is not grateful to Allah (reported by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī). Human kindness can be appreciated while its gifts are traced back to Allah.

The Arabic word Rabb can carry the sense of lord, caretaker, and sustainer, not merely a distant ruler. The Qur’an lets Moses explain this title to Pharaoh: “Lord of the heavens and earth and whatever is between them” (26:24). Calling Allah Rabb brings together authority, care, and the sustaining of what He created.

This phrase widens the horizon beyond one tribe, country, or generation. The Arabic plural al-ʿālamīn speaks broadly of the realms and kinds of creation. Allah is not Lord of one chosen corner only. The prayer can be spoken by people everywhere, each included among the creation that depends on Him.

These names return immediately after the praise of the previous verse, so Allah’s greatness is not presented as cold power. Their repetition makes mercy a steady theme, not a decorative opening. It places mercy beside the coming reminder of judgment. The worshipper is taught to hold Allah’s authority and mercy together.

The Arabic is recited with two established readings: Mālik, often rendered “Owner” or “Master,” and Malik, “King.” Both are preserved in Qur’anic recitation and emphasize Allah’s complete authority rather than contradicting one another. Human rulers hold limited power in this life. The verse points to the authority no one can challenge.

Yawm al-dīn is the day of recompense and judgment, when actions are brought into account. Qur’an 99:7-8 says a person will see even an atom’s weight of good or evil. Remembering that day gives moral weight to ordinary choices, while reassuring those whose deeds were hidden or overlooked.

The sentence turns from describing Allah to speaking directly to Him. In Arabic, “You” is placed before “we worship,” emphasizing that devotion is directed to Allah alone. Worship includes prayer, obedience, and humility. The Qur’an repeats the same call when it commands people to worship Allah and avoid false gods (16:36).

phrases.translation: and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help
phrases.explanation: The second half places reliance beside worship. Muslims can ask people for ordinary assistance, such as care, advice, or practical work, while recognizing that no created helper controls the outcome independently of Allah. The line also leads naturally into the next request: help is sought so the worshipper can find and follow the right path.

The request is made with “us,” not “me,” so the worshipper asks for guidance together with the community. Guidance means more than being shown a truth once. It includes being helped to recognize it, accept it, and remain steady. A believer repeats this prayer in salah without assuming that guidance is already secured.

The image is a road with a clear direction and destination. The prayer asks not for every desire to be granted, but to be led toward what pleases Allah and to keep moving there. The final verse explains this path through the lives of people who received Allah’s favor.

phrases.translation: the Path of those You have blessed
phrases.explanation: The next words explain what the Straight Path means: the way lived by people who obey Allah. Qur’an 4:69 names the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous among those whom Allah has favored. Their lives make guidance concrete, so the worshipper asks to follow a trustworthy way rather than invent one alone.

phrases.translation: not those You are displeased with
phrases.explanation: This phrase asks protection from choosing knowledge or status while turning away from what is right. It is a warning about a path and its outcome, not an invitation to label particular people or whole communities. Each person who recites it asks Allah to keep their own choices from bringing His displeasure.

The closing words ask protection from losing direction through ignorance, confusion, or following a false lead. Together with the previous phrase, they ask for both sound understanding and the will to act on it. The Qur’an gives a similar prayer: “Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us” (3:8).
